$comment:
A2A extension surface corpus, v0 — negotiation, honesty guard, placeholder guard, metadata placement.

WHY A CORPUS AND NOT TWO TEST FILES.
The same expectations written twice, once per language, is the defect this repo
has already been bitten by: an edit to one copy leaves the other green and the
divergence reaches a user instead of CI. Worse for THIS surface -- two SDKs that
agree with each other can still both be wrong about the protocol. One corpus,
both shipped implementations.

WHAT THE HONESTY VECTORS ARE FOR.
A banned-substring list is escapable by paraphrase. `aegis_backed_assurance` is
the exact paraphrase a reviewer produced when asked to defeat a banned-phrase
guard, and it is pinned here so the guard cannot regress to substring matching
and still look covered. The negated sentences are pinned for the opposite
reason: a guard that rejects its own disclaimer would push authors toward saying
nothing rather than saying the limit out loud.

negotiation.why: Extensions are inactive by default. Not an error -- but a NAMED outcome, so a caller can tell 'client did not opt in' from 'nothing to report'.
An empty header is the same as no header.
Another extension being requested must not activate this one.
Spec 14.2.2: comma-separated list. Whitespace around entries is not significant, and the other requested extensions are preserved in order.
Duplicates collapse; the echo is never a multiset.
Extension identifiers are matched exactly. Case-folding URIs would let a near-miss identifier silently activate a different vocabulary.

honesty.text: Reports Aegis boundary decisions using existing A2A TaskState values plus a substate in metadata. It is a reporting vocabulary: activating it does not enforce anything and is not proof that anything was enforced. Field names are carried; payload values are not. PRERELEASE: the identifier is a placeholder and is not registered.
honesty.why: The shipped description states the limit explicitly. A guard that rejects its own disclaimer would push authors toward silence.

honesty.text: Aegis-backed assurance active for this task.
honesty.why: The exact paraphrase produced when a reviewer was asked to defeat a banned-phrase list. Substring matching does not catch it.

honesty.text: Policy enforcement verified by the Aegis boundary.
honesty.why: Affirmative and unqualified.

honesty.text: This agent is protected by Aegis.
honesty.why: The claim the extension must never make on a counterparty's behalf.

honesty.text: The receipt is value-free.
honesty.why: Field-name sets, reason codes, counts and timings all disclose something. 'value-free' overstates it.

honesty.text: Carrying this extension does not mean access was enforced.
honesty.why: A negation is the honest form and must stay sayable.

honesty.text: Returns a list of restaurants near the requested location.
honesty.why: No claim, no subject. The guard must not fire on ordinary prose.

honesty.text: Aegis assurance active (readers remain unverified).
honesty.why: Round-1 cursor bypass: an unrelated negation-ish word APPENDED after the claim exempted it under the old any-negation-in-window rule. A negation only counts when it precedes the assurance term in the same sentence segment; 'unverified' is a status word, not a negation, and is no longer on the list at all.

honesty.text: The extension is not decorative; policy enforcement is verified.
honesty.why: Round-1 codex bypass: 'is not' in the FIRST clause exempted an affirmative claim in the second. Sentence-segment clipping stops the borrow — the claim clause contains no negation of its own.

honesty.text: This surface confirms Aegis coverage is in effect.
honesty.why: Round-1 cursor paraphrase outside the old assurance vocabulary. 'confirms', 'coverage' and 'in effect' are assurance words now.

honesty.text: The policy was verified for syntactic completeness only.
honesty.why: PINNED CONSERVATIVE BIAS, not an accident (round-1, both vendors flagged it as a false positive): on THIS surface an affirmative 'verified' about a policy is blocked even when the intended meaning is structural. The cost asymmetry is deliberate — a false block costs the producer a rephrase ('structure recomputed', 'schema-checked'); a false pass is enforcement fraud. Consumers derive verification status from deriveVerificationStatus, never from prose.

honesty.text: Aegis does not log, policy enforced.
honesty.why: Round-2 codex: a negation about LOGGING must not exempt a claim about ENFORCEMENT just because they share a sentence. Comma is a clause boundary now — the negation and the assurance it negates must share a clause.

honesty.text: This extension establishes that access was gated.
honesty.why: Round-3 cursor bypass: 'establishes'/'gated' were outside the vocabulary. Added.

honesty.text: Aegis upholds the access policy for this task.
honesty.why: Round-3 cursor bypass: 'upholds' added.

honesty.text: Policy ｖｅｒｉｆｉｅｄ by the Aegis boundary.
honesty.why: Round-3 cursor P1: the honesty guard now NFKC-normalizes, so a full-width 'verified' folds to ASCII and is caught — parity with the key normalizer.

honesty.text: Records were certified inaccessible.
honesty.why: Round-3 cursor P1 (cause corrected): substring matching found the SUBJECT 'access' inside 'inaccessible', so 'certified ... inaccessible' fired with no real subject present. Word-boundary matching fixes it — 'inaccessible' is not the word 'access', and with no genuine subject the assurance word 'certified' does not fire. (A sentence naming a real subject near an affirmative assurance word is still blocked by the pinned conservative bias.)

honesty.text: Our SOC 2 report confirms coverage of access-control reviews.
honesty.why: Round-3 cursor P1 false positive: 'confirms' and 'coverage' were too broad and hit honest compliance prose. Dropped as standalone assurance words; the round-1 case they guarded is still caught by 'in effect'.

honesty.text: Aegis blocks unauthorized access.
honesty.why: Round-3 codex bypass: 'blocks'/'prevents' added. 'Aegis blocks access' is an enforcement claim this extension must never make.

honesty.text: The policy establishes the document format.
honesty.why: Round-3 codex false positive: 'establishes' was too generic (dropped). This honest sentence about document format no longer trips; cursor's 'establishes that access was gated' is still caught via 'gated'.

honesty.text: This extension establishes that access was gated.
honesty.why: Confirms dropping 'establishes' did not reopen cursor's round-3 bypass: 'gated' near 'access'/'extension' still fires.

placeholder.why: The shipped identifier is a placeholder and must be detectable as one until an owner registers a real URI.
What a registered identifier would look like. Pinned so the guard is falsifiable rather than 'always true'.

metadata_placement.why: Spec 4.6.1/4.6.2: metadata is keyed BY the extension URI, and unrelated metadata is left alone.
Writing extension metadata a client never opted into is the quiet version of the disclosure problem.
Emission is the other half of round 3/A2: this SDK must be unable to PRODUCE the producer-asserted trust field its consumer side exists to reject.

substate.note: Policy enforcement verified by the Aegis boundary.

metadata_placement.why: Round-1 critique (both vendors): the privacy validator must sit ON the emission path, not beside it. An unknown key dies before the wire — which also closes the free-text covert channel it would have carried.
H-006 at the producer: the documented mapping-to-placement flow was the exact path that shipped 'alice' to the wire. Emission now validates provenance itself.
The guarded path must still WORK: declared field names pass, and the emission guards do not block the honest vocabulary.

Round-1 codex: a sibling coreVerified in the caller's own metadata must not be couriered onto the wire. The carrier is scanned for trust-assertion keys at the top level and inside non-namespace nested objects; other extensions' URI-keyed bags are left opaque (see other_extension_bag_preserved).

H-003's runtime mutant at the emission door, updated for layered guards: with the key vocabulary closed, the remaining string carrier is a value inside a LEGAL field whose provenance the caller poisoned (a declared 'role label' that is really a claim). The honesty walk over runtime string values is the layer that catches it.

Round-2 both vendors: A2A permits independently typed extension metadata, and 'authenticated' is a perfectly legal word in someone ELSE'S vocabulary. Recursing Aegis's reserved-key policy into other extensions' URI bags made this SDK incompatible with innocent co-installed extensions. Their bags are opaque; only the carrier's TOP-LEVEL keys and OUR value are policed.

existing_metadata.note: The access policy was verified last quarter.

expect_preserves.note: The access policy was verified last quarter.

metadata_placement.why: Round-2 cursor: the caller's own prose is the caller's own claim — this SDK polices what IT emits (its value, and machine-readable authority keys at the top level), not the integrator's unrelated notes. The honesty guard applies to our value only.
Round-2 liveness fix, wire half: the buildObligationStatusUpdate output places cleanly, so a poller can distinguish a denied-and-waiting AUTH_REQUIRED from an actionable one.
Round-3 cursor P1: the round-2 top-level-only scan left a depth-1 courier hole. 'notes' is not a namespace, so its contents ARE scanned — a nested coreVerified is refused just like a top-level one.

The opacity is by NAMESPACE, at any depth: a trust word nested arbitrarily deep inside ANOTHER extension's URI bag is still theirs, and stays untouched. Only the round-3 nested-courier hole (non-namespace parents) is closed.

Round-3 codex P2: a top-level 'authenticated: false' from the integrator's own auth system is not an Aegis authority claim. The carrier scan uses the NARROW impersonation list, so generic fields pass; only keys naming OUR output are refused.

'enforced' names this extension's never-claim directly — a sibling 'enforced: true' would read as 'Aegis enforced this task'. It is in the narrow impersonation list and refused, even though 'authenticated' is not.
The narrow scan still recurses into non-namespace nested objects: a nested enforcementStatus impersonates our output at depth 1 and is refused.
